source_text: Οἱ γὰρ Θεὸν ἀγνοήσαντες, αἰτίαν ἔμφρονα προεστάναι τῆς γενέσεως τῶν ὅλων οὐ συνεχώρησαν, ἀλλ' οἰκείως τῇ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἀγνοίᾳ τὰ ἐφεξῆς συνεπέραναν. Διὰ τοῦτο οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ τὰς ὑλικὰς ὑποθέσεις κατέφυγον, τοῖς τοῦ κόσμου στοιχείοις τὴν αἰτίαν τοῦ παντὸς ἀναθέντες· οἱ δὲ ἄτομα καὶ ἀμερῆ σώματα, καὶ ὄγκους καὶ πόρους συνέχειν τὴν φύσιν τῶν ὁρατῶν ἐφαντάσθησαν. Νῦν μὲν γὰρ συνιόντων ἀλλήλοις τῶν ἀμερῶν σωμάτων, νῦν δὲ μετασυγκρινομένων, τὰς γενέσεις καὶ τὰς φθορὰς ἐπιγίνεσθαι· καὶ τῶν διαρκεσ τέρων σωμάτων τὴν ἰσχυροτέραν τῶν ἀτόμων ἀντεμπλοκὴν τῆς διαμονῆς τὴν αἰτίαν παρέχειν. Ὄντως ἱστὸν ἀράχνης ὑφαίνουσιν οἱ ταῦτα γράφοντες, οἱ οὕτω λεπτὰς καὶ ἀνυπο στάτους ἀρχὰς οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς καὶ θαλάσσης ὑποτιθέμενοι. Οὐ γὰρ ᾔδεσαν εἰπεῖν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεὸς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. Διὰ τοῦτο ἀκυβέρνητα καὶ ἀδιοίκητα εἶναι τὰ σύμπαντα, ὡς ἂν τύχῃ φερόμενα, ὑπὸ τῆς ἐνοικούσης αὐτοῖς ἀθεότητος ἠπατήθησαν. Ὅπερ ἵνα μὴ πάθωμεν ἡμεῖς, ὁ τὴν κοσμοποιίαν συγγράφων εὐθὺς ἐν τοῖς πρώτοις ῥήμασι τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ Θεοῦ τὴν διάνοιαν ἡμῶν κατεφώ τισεν, εἰπὼν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεός. Τί καλὴ ἡ τάξις; Ἀρχὴν πρῶτον ἐπέθηκεν, ἵνα μὴ ἄναρχον αὐτὸν οἰηθῶσί τινες. Εἶτα ἐπήγαγε τὸ, Ἐποίησεν, ἵνα δειχθῇ, ὅτι ἐλάχιστον μέρος τῆς τοῦ δημιουργοῦ δυνάμεώς ἐστι τὸ ποιηθέν. Ὡς γὰρ ὁ κεραμεὺς ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς τέχνης μυρία διαπλάσας σκεύη, οὔτε τὴν τέχνην οὔτε δύναμιν ἐξανάλωσεν· οὕτω καὶ ὁ τοῦ παντὸς τούτου δημιουργὸς, οὐχ ἑνὶ κόσμῳ σύμμετρον τὴν ποιητικὴν ἔχων δύναμιν, ἀλλ' εἰς τὸ ἀπειροπλάσιον ὑπερβαίνουσαν, τῇ ῥοπῇ τοῦ θελήματος μόνῃ εἰς τὸ εἶναι παρήγαγε τὰ μεγέθη τῶν ὁρωμένων. Εἰ οὖν καὶ ἀρχὴν ἔχει ὁ κόσμος, καὶ πεποίηται, ζήτει, τίς ὁ τὴν ἀρχὴν αὐτῷ δοὺς, καὶ τίς ὁ ποιητής; Μᾶλλον δὲ, ἵνα μὴ ἀνθρωπίνοις λογισμοῖς ἐκζητῶν παρατραπῇς που τῆς ἀληθείας, προέφθασε τῇ διδασκαλίᾳ, οἱονεὶ σφραγῖδα καὶ φυλακτήριον ταῖς ψυχαῖς ἡμῶν ἐμβαλὼν τὸ πολυτίμητον ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ, εἰπὼν, Ἐν ἀρχῇ ἐποίησεν ὁ Θεός. Ἡ μακαρία φύσις, ἡ ἄφθονος ἀγαθότης, τὸ ἀγαπητὸν πᾶσι τοῖς λόγου μετειληφόσι, τὸ πολυπόθητον κάλλος, ἡ ἀρχὴ τῶν ὄντων, ἡ πηγὴ τῆς ζωῆς, τὸ νοερὸν φῶς, ἡ ἀπρόσιτος σοφία, οὗτος Ἐποίησεν ἐν ἀρχῇ τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ τὴν γῆν. 1.3 Μὴ οὖν ἄναρχα φαντάζου, ἄνθρωπε, τὰ ὁρώμενα, μηδὲ, ἐπειδὴ κυκλόσε περιτρέχει τὰ κατ' οὐρανὸν κινούμενα, ἡ δὲ τοῦ κύκλου ἀρχὴ τῇ προχείρῳ αἰσθήσει ἡμῶν οὐκ εὔληπτος, ἄναρχον εἶναι νομίσῃς τῶν κυκλοφορικῶν σωμάτων τὴν φύσιν. Οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ κύκλος οὗτος, τὸ ἐπίπεδον λέγω σχῆμα τὸ ὑπὸ μιᾶς γραμμῆς περιεχόμενον, ἐπειδὴ διαφεύγει τὴν ἡμετέραν αἴσθησιν, καὶ οὔτε ὅθεν ἤρξατο ἐξευρεῖν δυνάμεθα, οὔτε εἰς ὃ κατέληξεν, ἤδη καὶ ἄναρχον αὐτὸν ὀφείλομεν ὑποτίθεσθαι. Ἀλλὰ κἂν τὴν αἴσθησιν διαφεύγῃ, τῇ γε ἀληθείᾳ πάντως ἀπό τινος ἤρξατο ὁ κέντρῳ καὶ διαστήματί τινι περιγράψας αὐτόν. Οὕτω καὶ σὺ μὴ, ἐπειδὴ εἰς ἑαυτὰ συννεύει τὰ κύκλῳ κινούμενα, τὸ τῆς κινήσεως αὐτῶν ὁμαλὸν, καὶ μηδενὶ μέσῳ διακοπτόμενον, τὴν τοῦ ἄναρχον τὸν κόσμον καὶ ἀτελεύτητον εἶναί σοι πλάνην ἐγκαταλίπῃ.
thought_title: The world's beginning refutes godless cosmologies
orientation: Basil is expounding Genesis 1:1, arguing against Greek philosophers who denied that an intelligent cause stands over the origin of all things.
pass_a_gloss: For those who did not know God did not allow that an intelligent cause stood over the origin of all things, but in a way consistent with their ignorance from the beginning they drew the subsequent conclusions. For this reason some fled to material principles, attributing the cause of everything to the elements of the world; others imagined that atoms and indivisible bodies and masses and pores hold together the nature of visible things. For now when the indivisible bodies come together with one another, now when they are recombined, the origins and destructions come about; and the stronger interweaving of the atoms provides the cause of the permanence of the more enduring bodies. Truly those who write these things weave a spider's web, those who posit such fine and insubstantial principles of heaven and earth and sea. For they did not know how to say, In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. For this reason they were deceived by the godlessness dwelling in them into thinking that all things are unsteered and ungoverned, carried along as chance would have it. So that we might not suffer this, the one who wrote the account of the world's creation immediately in the first words illuminated our mind with the name of God, saying, In the beginning God made. How beautiful is the order! He placed beginning first, so that some might not think it without beginning. Then he added, He made, so that it might be shown that what was made is the smallest part of the Creator's power. For just as the potter, having shaped countless vessels from the same craft, exhausted neither the craft nor the power; so also the Creator of this universe, having a creative power not measured to one world but surpassing it to an infinite degree, by the inclination of his will alone brought into being the magnitudes of visible things. If therefore the world has a beginning and has been made, seek who is the one who gave it the beginning, and who is the maker? But rather, so that you might not be turned aside somewhere from the truth by seeking with human reasonings, he anticipated with the teaching, placing in our souls as it were a seal and a safeguard the precious name of God, saying, In the beginning God made. The blessed nature, the ungrudging goodness, the beloved of all who have received a share of reason, the much-longed-for beauty, the beginning of beings, the source of life, the intellectual light, the unapproachable wisdom, this one made in the beginning the heaven and the earth. Do not then imagine, O man, that visible things are without beginning, nor, since the things moving in heaven run around in a circle and the beginning of the circle is not easily grasped by our ready perception, think that the nature of the circular-moving bodies is without beginning. For not even this circle, I mean the plane figure enclosed by one line, because it escapes our perception, and we are able to discover neither where it began nor where it ended, must we therefore suppose it to be without beginning. But even if it escapes perception, in truth it certainly began from some point, the one who drew it with a center and some radius. So also you, since the things moving in a circle turn back upon themselves, do not let the evenness of their motion, interrupted by no middle point, leave in you the error that the world is without beginning and without end.

choices.why: Keeps the adjective as attributive to cause, matching Basil's contrast between a rational cause and material principles.
Renders the philosophical term for foundational material causes, preserving the technical sense.
Keeps the proverbial image of fragile, insubstantial construction, matching Basil's rhetorical dismissal.
Preserves the two distinct adjectives: lack of a pilot (κυβερνήτης) and lack of administration (διοίκησις).

choices.why: Renders ῥοπή as the decisive tilt or inclination of will, emphasizing effortless creation.

pass_b_english: Those who did not know God would not allow that an intelligent cause stood over the origin of all things, but drew their conclusions in a way consistent with their initial ignorance. For this reason some fled to material principles, assigning the cause of everything to the elements of the world; others imagined that atoms and partless bodies, masses and pores, hold together the nature of visible things. Now, they said, when the partless bodies come together with one another, and now when they are rearranged, births and destructions come about; and in the case of the more enduring bodies, the stronger interweaving of the atoms provides the cause of their permanence. Truly those who write these things weave a spider's web, setting up such fine and insubstantial principles for heaven and earth and sea. For they did not know how to say, “In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1). Because of this they were deceived by the godlessness dwelling within them into thinking that all things are unsteered and ungoverned, carried along as chance would have it. So that we might not suffer this, the one who wrote the account of the world's creation at once, in his very first words, illuminated our minds with the name of God, saying, “In the beginning God made.” How beautiful is the order! He placed “beginning” first, so that no one would think the world is without beginning. Then he added “made,” so that it might be shown that what was made is the smallest part of the Creator's power. For just as a potter, having shaped countless vessels by the same art, has not used up either his art or his power, so also the Creator of this universe does not have a creative power measured to one world alone, but one that surpasses it to an infinite degree, and by the inclination of his will alone he brought the magnitudes of visible things into being. If then the world has a beginning and has been made, ask who gave it its beginning and who is its maker. Or rather, so that you may not be led astray from the truth by searching with human reasonings, he anticipated you with his teaching, placing in our souls as a seal and a safeguard the precious name of God, saying, “In the beginning God made.” The blessed nature, the ungrudging goodness, the one beloved by all who have received reason, the much-longed-for beauty, the beginning of all beings, the source of life, the intelligible light, the unapproachable wisdom—this one “made the heaven and the earth in the beginning” (Genesis 1:1). Do not imagine, then, O man, that visible things are without beginning; and do not suppose, because the things that move in the heavens run round in a circle and the beginning of a circle is not easily grasped by our ordinary perception, that the nature of the bodies that move in circles is without beginning. For this circle—I mean the plane figure enclosed by a single line—even though it escapes our perception, and we cannot discover where it began or where it ended, we are not therefore obliged to suppose that it is without beginning. But even if it escapes perception, in truth it certainly began from some point, drawn by one who marked it out with a center and a radius. So you too, because the things that move in a circle return upon themselves, do not let the smoothness of their motion, uninterrupted by anything in the middle, leave in you the error that the world is without beginning and without end.

problems.why: νοερὸν means 'intelligible' or 'intellectual', not 'spiritual'; this is a key philosophical term.
problems.ruling: νοερὸν means 'intelligible/intellectual', not 'spiritual'; mistranslates a key patristic philosophical term.

fixed: Changed 'the spiritual light' to 'the intelligible light' because νοερὸν means 'intelligible' or 'intellectual', not 'spiritual'.

last_rejected.quote: the one beloved by all who have received reason
last_rejected.source_quote: τὸ ἀγαπητὸν πᾶσι τοῖς λόγου μετειληφόσι
last_rejected.why: λόγου here means 'word/reason' but μετειληφόσι means 'partaken of/shared in', not 'received'; 'received reason' suggests acquisition of rational faculty rather than participation in the Logos/reason
last_rejected.fix: the one beloved by all who have partaken of reason
last_rejected.ruling: μετειληφόσι = 'having received/partaken of'; 'received reason' is within normal range for λόγου μετειληφόσι.

last_rejected.quote: by the inclination of his will alone
last_rejected.why: ῥοπή means 'inclination/leaning/turning' but in context of divine creation it conveys effortless impulse; 'inclination' is too weak, suggesting a mere tendency rather than decisive act
last_rejected.fix: by the mere bent of his will
last_rejected.ruling: ῥοπή normally means 'inclination/leaning'; rendering as 'inclination' is standard, not a meaning change or loss.
